_comment: seccomp-agent.json — a HAND-WRITTEN seccomp profile that tries to sandbox the
evil agent the way you would today with Docker: deny the syscalls an exfiltrating
process needs. This is the strongest honest version of the 'Docker already does
this' rebuttal — and it is exactly what the Axon flagship demo is contrasted with.
THE AGENT HAS THREE ESCAPES: (1) read /etc/passwd, (2) open a network socket,
(3) spawn a process. A seccomp profile can cleanly block only ONE of them:
(2) network  — DENY `socket`/`connect`. Clean: CPython doesn't need them to boot.
(3) process  — you'd DENY `execve`, but Docker LAUNCHES the container WITH execve,
so denying it means the container never starts ('exec ...: operation not
permitted'). seccomp is stateless: it cannot say 'exec once to start, then
never spawn a child.' So in practice execve stays ALLOWED and the spawn survives.
(1) file     — you'd DENY `openat`, but `openat` is load-bearing: CPython opens
dozens of files just to start, so denying it kills the interpreter. seccomp
filters SYSCALLS, not PATHS — it has no way to say 'open anything except
/etc/passwd.' So openat stays ALLOWED and the secret read survives.
Net result: this profile blocks 1 of 3 escapes; the other 2 survive because a
syscall filter is too blunt to express the actual policy. Axon's
@[contained(fs: [], net: [], exec: none)] blocks ALL THREE at COMPILE TIME, because
the policy is expressed over capabilities, not raw syscall numbers.
This profile is also a SEPARATE ARTIFACT from the agent's code: nothing keeps the two
in sync. Edit the agent to need a new capability and this file silently stays wrong
(over- or under-permissioned) until a human remembers to update it. Axon derives the
syscall allowlist FROM the code (.axmeta syscall_hint), so it cannot drift.

syscalls.comment: deny network (the ai_complete / urllib exfil channel) — the one escape seccomp blocks cleanly
